data.title: IQVIA Launches IQVIA Life Science Models to Help Life Sciences Companies Predict Clinical Trial Outcomes
data.description:
RESEARCH TRIANGLE PARK, N.C. —

October 7, 2026 – IQVIA (NYSE:IQV), a leading global provider of clinical research services, commercial insights and healthcare intelligence to the life sciences and healthcare industries, today at TechIQ 2026 introduced IQVIA Life Science Models™ to help predict clinical trial outcomes.

IQVIA Life Science Models are a suite of purpose-built models for life sciences, combining IQVIA’s proprietary expert content, deep domain knowledge and established regulatory, compliance and privacy frameworks. Built using technologies including NVIDIA Nemotron™ and supported by Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure, the models connect molecular and treatment information with patient journeys and clinical outcomes to enable predictive applications across clinical development. 

  • Clinical study simulation and protocol optimization, including endpoint selection, patient eligibility criteria, dose selection and sample size planning, helping teams identify risks before trials begin. In initial evaluation across 50 trials and 270 endpoints, 85% of predictions were on target or clinically close.
  • Digital twins and synthetic controls that support more efficient study designs. 
  • Leverage clinical study predictions to inform better real-world planning and access.

In clinical development, Life Science Models extend IQVIA’s Predictive Clinical Development approach, enabling sponsors to simulate studies and test key assumptions before execution, helping optimize study design and identify potential risks earlier.

To learn more, visit IQVIA Life Science Models.

data.title: The top biopharma conferences in 2027
data.description:
Clinical trial results are the key events that make or break a biotechnology company. Positive data can validate a drugmaker’s business plan and boost its stock price, while a disappointing readout can change its course. These crucial findings are often presented and closely analyzed at medical conferences throughout the year — meetings where companies get to showcase the medicines they’ve staked their futures on. 

These conferences have different focuses. Some spotlight early research or the final trials that can yield regulatory approvals. Others are temperature takers for the industry’s health, where companies and investors gather to network and cut deals. 

Below, BioPharma Dive has collected schedules for the key medical meetings and conferences planned for 2027. 

 

Top medical and industry meetings in 2027

 

J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference

Jan. 11-14
San Francisco

Every year, biopharma investors and executives descend on San Francisco’s Union Square to talk deals. With luck, a handful of companies will have new acquisitions or partnerships to announce during the meeting’s first few days — M&A activity that could be a harbinger of what's to come in the year ahead.

BIO Investment & Growth Summit

Feb. 16-17
Miami

A meeting once called the CEO and Investor Conference and hosted in New York will be held in Miami Beach under a newer name in 2027. Still, the gathering will have an investor focus, with networking opportunities for biotechnology CEOs and their backers.  

MDA Clinical & Scientific Conference

March 21-24
Orlando, Florida

Hosted by the Muscular Dystrophy Association, a prominent patient advocacy group, the meeting showcases promising research in neuromuscular disease and brings together industry leaders, physicians and scientists to discuss important clinical trial results and real-world data. 

American Association for Cancer Research Annual Meeting

April 2-7
Orlando, Florida

While the American Society of Clinical Oncology’s meeting often gets billed as the field’s largest conference, AACR has become an equally major gathering for cancer science, particularly earlier-stage findings on new drug mechanisms of action or treatment modalities.

American College of Cardiology Annual Scientific Session

April 10-12
Houston

The growing body of evidence showing that GLP-1 medicines can affect a variety of cardiometabolic conditions, and the sheer number of clinical trials underway in obesity, makes ACC a meeting likely to feature presentations that inform the field’s direction. 

American Academy of Neurology Annual Meeting

May 1-5
Washington, D.C.

AAN often features the latest findings in research for diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s, making it one of the top forums for assessing recent progress in neuroscience.

American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy Annual Meeting

May 3-7
Philadelphia 

ASGCT has grown with the cell and gene therapy field, becoming a premier conference as the sector expanded and treatments advanced further into human testing. While such therapies still offer much promise, the difficulties companies face successfully marketing them have made the meeting a health check for the sector as well.

American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting

June 4-8
Chicago

ASCO is a lodestone for cancer drug research with the highest profile and widest impact. The data presented each year at McCormick Place in Chicago often changes treatment standards, as well as makes (or breaks) the fortunes of drug developers.

BIO International Convention

June 7-10
Philadelphia

BIO’s International Convention is always an important convener for biotech and pharma companies’ business development teams. It’s also regularly a venue for industry leaders to discuss and debate the top challenges facing the sector.

European Hematology Association Congress

June 10-13
Barcelona, Spain

EHA is one of the year’s biggest meetings devoted specifically to hematology and includes results at the forefront of research into leukemias, lymphomas and non-malignant blood diseases like sickle cell disease.  

European Association for the Study of the Liver Congress

June 16-19
London

From hepatitis C to MASH, the burden of liver diseases is large and costly. Europe’s main hepatology meeting is an international forum for the latest research into these disorders as clinicians present data on risk factors and new treatment approaches.

American Diabetes Association’s Scientific Sessions

June 18-21
Washington, D.C.

ADA is one of the largest medical meetings focused on diabetes and frequently features new research on the care and treatment of differing patient populations with the condition.

European Society of Cardiology Annual Congress

Aug. 27-30
Milan

ESC brings together tens of thousands of cardiology experts to discuss practice-changing research in heart disease. The meeting has been a recent venue for important study results from Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, Novo Nordisk and AstraZeneca, among other companies.

World Conference on Lung Cancer

Sept. 11-14
Denver

WCLC is the world’s top conference on advances in lung cancer, one of the most competitive areas in oncology and a coveted market among drugmakers. Over the last couple years, the WCLC has been the forum for advances among a closely watched group of cancer immunotherapies called PD-1/VEGF inhibitors, which could change the way many lung tumors are treated. 

European Society for Medical Oncology Congress

Sept. 17-21
Barcelona, Spain

ESMO is Europe’s answer to the American Society of Clinical Oncology’s annual meeting and just as often features standard-shifting cancer research. While immunotherapy remains an active area of exploration for drugmakers, increasingly other treatment types like antibody-drug conjugates and radiopharmaceuticals have been featured at oncology conferences.

European Association for the Study of Diabetes

Sept. 20-24
Budapest, Hungary

The EASD meeting is another important showcase for the “incretin” diabetes and weight loss medicines that have soared in popularity in recent years. The 2026 edition spotlighted a wave of next-generation obesity therapies, among them a treatment that could help Eli Lilly extend its market-leading franchise. 

36th European Academy of Dermatology & Venereology Congress

Sept. 22-25
Amsterdam

EADV showcases the latest research into skin diseases like atopic dermatitis, which has become a top battleground for drug research as companies look for ways to improve upon Sanofi and Regeneron Pharmaceuticals’ top-selling Dupixent. 

The Liver Meeting

TBD
TBD

Thousands of hepatology professionals gather each year at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases’ annual meeting.

American Heart Association Scientific Sessions

Nov. 5-8
Boston

AHA is always a major forum for the latest research on medicines to treat diseases of the heart.

20th Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease

TBD
TBD

Focused on medicines for Alzheimer’s disease, CTAD hosts scientists and experts in the field to discuss new treatment approaches for the neurological condition.

American Society of Hematology Annual Meeting

TBD
TBD

This meeting regularly features compelling new research on treatments for diseases of the blood, from cancers to non-malignant disorders like sickle cell and beta thalassemia.

data.title: Precision for All: Closing the gap between innovation and impact
data.description:
Diagnostic-driven therapies are being discovered and developed faster than ever, yet too many eligible patients never receive the treatments that could help them.

Today, due to complex diagnostic workflows, evolving testing protocols, and structural access barriers across care settings, eligible patients are frequently lost along the treatment journey.  This is not a failure of science—it is a breakdown in care pathways and commercial execution. It's also an increasingly common problem for in-market therapies, as well as new and emerging ones.

In one example, Diaceutics published research has shown that in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (aNSCLC), a disease where targeted therapy exists and should be benefiting patients, approximately 64% of eligible patients do not receive the appropriate targeted therapy. Roughly 29% are lost from the pathway even after a diagnostic test has successfully identified the actionable biomarker.

Closing these gaps requires a new commercialization model, one that helps biopharma teams strengthen diagnostic readiness, improve testing consistency and availability, educate healthcare providers and connect eligible patients with the right treatment.

Diagnostic-driven therapies are therapies where diagnostic activity influences whether, when, or how patients reach treatment. In other words, they are therapies where diagnostic intelligence creates a competitive advantage.

How to Close the Gaps

Science has already transformed what's possible. What's been missing is a commercialization model built explicitly to match it—and the collective will to change. Now is the time for the industry to address these gaps, ensuring that more patients receive the therapy they need.

Closing the gap doesn't require a bigger version of the old model—it requires a different one.

First, persistent practice gaps must be identified in real time, using real-world data and insights to see exactly where and why patients are being lost across the pathway.

Secondly, diagnostic infrastructure—laboratories and testing networks—must be supported to reduce variability in ordering, panels, and turnaround times.

Thirdly, treating clinicians must be given clear, contextual support at the moment intention becomes action.

This isn’t an aspirational model, it’s already in place. Diaceutics has made a positive impact on engagement and interventions for a wide range of brands across numerous therapy areas, pre-launch (36%), launch (20%) and 3 years post launch (44%).

For example, Diaceutics has shown that a program of precision outreach and real-world data can transform rare disease management for a childhood rare disease. By enabling timely engagement with physicians, Diaceutics helped accelerate therapy adoption for an in-market therapy, improve patient access, and support more equitable care for a highly underserved population. The program identified 121 patients eligible for a therapy, generating $2M in revenue and a 70% ROI.

Across its work with biopharma companies, these approaches have delivered a 35% uplift in new therapy starts, an 8% increase in market share within 12 months for a top 10 pharmaceutical company, and a 19% increase in actionable care targets. These results demonstrate what is possible when diagnostic, commercial, medical, and market access functions work from a shared understanding of where patients are being lost and how to close those gaps.

Turn diagnostic intelligence into commercial action

This is the model Diaceutics has built its Intelligence and Engagement Solutions around. Powered by Diaceutics' Reveal data engine, its solutions connect real-world diagnostic activity with the intelligence and engagement to see where eligible patients are being missed, act while treatment decisions are forming and help more people reach the right therapy.

  • Intelligence Solutions uncover where diagnostic activity is creating opportunity—where patients are being missed, which HCPs shape care, and which labs can change the pathway.
  • Engagement Solutions help reach the people who can move that pathway forward—through targeted HCP marketing, scientific exchange and lab engagement at the moment that matters.

The shift these solutions enable is important: from looking retrospectively at what happened, to acting prospectively on what's happening now.

Diaceutics: Life unlocked

Diaceutics is the intelligence and engagement company unlocking the full potential for diagnostic-driven therapies. It helps biopharma teams find eligible patients earlier, understand where diagnostic pathways break down, and act while treatment decisions are still forming.

Diaceutics has spent more than 20 years working at the intersection of diagnostics and commercialization and today works with biopharma companies ranging from emerging biotech to 21 of the world's top 30 pharma companies.

Precision for All

Science has given us the ability to identify increasingly precise patient populations and develop therapies specifically for them. The next challenge is ensuring our commercialization models are equally precise.

That's the ambition behind Precision for All: a future where every eligible patient is identified, diagnosed and receives the right therapy at the right time.

Getting there will require biopharma, diagnostics, HCPs, labs, and health systems to close the gaps between innovation and impact together. The technology, data and expertise exist, the opportunity now is to put them to work.

It's time to make precision the standard for all, not the privilege of the few.

data.title: Archō’s ELAVAY Cardiometabolic Report Names Eli Lilly the Company Diabetes Advocates Trust Most
data.description:
MOUNT PLEASANT`, S.C. —

Archō Advocacy today released the 2025/2026 ELAVAY Cardiometabolic Advocacy Intelligence Report, the annual read on which companies diabetes and cardiometabolic advocates, professional societies, and community-based organizations trust to act in the patient interest. Eli Lilly finishes first, or ties for first, in six of the eight measured categories and places in the top three of every one. Dexcom finishes first in health equity and in advocacy relationships, ahead of every pharmaceutical company in the study.

Twelve companies earned mentions across the cardiometabolic field: Eli Lilly, Dexcom, Abbott Diabetes Care, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi, Insulet Corporation, Medtronic, Tandem Diabetes Care, Merck, Novartis, Genentech/Roche, and Vertex. Continuous glucose monitor and insulin pump makers share the league table with drug makers here, and they take more of the top three positions than pharma does.

“Diabetes advocates spend their days with the companies that touch the patient every day. Eli Lilly won this report by funding the work and then gett ing out of the way. Thee device companies won their positions by showing up in the community long before they needed anything,” said Matt Toresco, Founder and CEO of Archō Advocacy.

WHO LEADS, AND WHERE

Advocates ranked the companies they had worked with in the past 12 to 18 months, then rated their top three on a seven-point scale. Archō weighted recognition against rating to build each league table. Thee leaders follow, and the full report carries the scores behind them.

Corporation wins the one measure that sits outside the league tables. On the Scale of Selflessness, which asks advocates how transparent a company is about what it wants from the relationship, Insulet scores a perfect 7.00, the only perfect score in the report. Eli Lilly follows at 6.50 and Novo Nordisk at 6.00. Insulet turns that goodwill into a top-three finnish nowhere else, because too few advocates have worked with it.

Two results explain the shape of this field. Sanofi earns the highest average rating in both Partnerships and Government Policy, 6.33 and 6.13, and finishes fifth in each, because only a third of advocates named it at all. Medtronic posts a 6.00 average in Partnerships and finishes last. In cardiometabolic care, a strong relationship with a few organizations does not win a category.

THE DEVICE COMPANIES CHANGED THE TABLE

Dexcom, Abbott Diabetes Care, Insulet Corporation, Medtronic, and Tandem Diabetes Care all place in this report, and the first three outrank most of the pharmaceutical field. Dexcom finishes first in health equity contribution and first on advocacy relationships, ahead of every drug maker measured. Abbott Diabetes Care ties for first on RISE (Reach, Include, Support & Educate) recognition and holds third in Partnerships, Corporate Image, and Health Equity. No other ELAVAY therapeutic report looks like this.

Advocates explain the gap in operating terms rather than brand terms. “Dexcom has done a good job at connecting us with like-minded organizations to coordinate advocacy messaging,” one wrote. On equity, another credited the technology directly: “Dexcom is very concerned with the improvements in health that CGM offers all people with diabetes. They are leading in affordability of CGM for all.” Abbott earns credit for work the industry usually avoids: “Abbott has led a campaign on diabetes stigma which seeks to improve how people with diabetes are treated.”

Thee device field also draws the sharpest criticism in the dataset. One advocate described a sponsor relationship this way: “Constantly obscuring their pipeline, connecting funding to helping get their sales messaging amplified, strongly advocating for changes in our messaging to align with theirs.” Proximity to the patient cuts both ways.

“In diabetes, the company in the room every day is the one making the sensor or the pump. Advocates score that access honestly. Dexcom and Abbott earned rank by doing the unglamorous work, and the pharmaceutical companies that outspend them still finished behind them,” said Matt Toresco, Founder and CEO of Archō.

WHY ELI LILLY WINS: FUNDING WITHOUT A LEASH

Eli Lilly finishes first, or ties for first, in six categories and never falls below third in any measured table. Advocates describe the same behavior across those six. Thee company funds the work the organization already planned, and it does not attach the funding to its own message.

“Lilly consistently funds these initiatives with no expectation of deliverables or benefits to them commercially,” wrote one diabetes advocacy leader. Another described the working relationship: “Lilly folks ask us what they can do to help amplify our patient centered messaging including psychosocial aspects of diabetes.” A third put the reason for the reputation score plainly: “Lilly leads with kindness and empathy for patients and our members.” On access, advocates name a specific decision rather than a program: “Lilly was a leader in insulin pricing reductions and supports access and affordability in other products as well.”

CARDIOMETABOLIC ADVOCATES BREAK WITH THE FIELD ON THE IRA

Advocates in this space expect the Inflation Reduction Act to help their patients. Four in five anticipate a positive effeect, and the rest expect no effeect either way. Not one expects harm. Oncology and mental health advocates land nowhere near that position in the same study year, which makes cardiometabolic the outlier in the 2025/2026 dataset. 

Thee engagement behind that view is real. More than eight in ten respondents work on healthcare policy inside their organizations, and two thirds educate their communities about the law through coalitions rather than alone. Half run federal lobbying, and half run state lobbying.

Priorities still sit closer to the exam room than to Washington. Two thirds rank disease awareness and education as the single most important challenge facing their patients, the widest first-place margin of any issue in the report. Two thirds call non-medical medication switching a high or extremely high threat, while a third report no opinion at all, a split worth watching. Half of these organizations say workforce and budget reductions across the industry have signifincantly reduced collaboration with them.

“Diabetes advocates read the Inflation Reduction Act as a win for the patients they represent, and they are the only community in this year’s study that does. Theat gap matt ers. A company running one federal policy message across every therapeutic area is gett ing it wrong in at least two of them,” Toresco said.

FROM INSIGHT TO ACTION: THE ADVOCACY INFLUENCE DIAGNOSTIC

ELAVAY measures how the outside world sees a company. Its companion tool, the Advocacy Influence Diagnostic (AID), measures how a company’s own organization sees and uses its advocacy function. AID sorts advocacy leaders into four personas, the Architect, the Defender, the Underdog, and the Whisperer, and surfaces where internal influence lags external rank.“A device company can outrank the pharmaceutical field outside and still lose the budget argument inside. AID tells advocacy leaders where their internal stance trails their external reputation, where to fix it, and how we can help at Archō,” said Toresco.

Thee full 2025/2026 ELAVAY Cardiometabolic Report carries every league table, the ratings behind each rank, and the advocate testimony in full. For the report or a private briefing on where a company sits inside the dataset, visit https://archo.io or contact Matt Toresco at [email protected].

data.title: Cresset launches Flare AI Client, helping computational chemists complete hours of work in minutes
data.description:
CAMBRIDGE, United Kingdom —

Scientists can now connect company-approved AI providers such as Claude Code and GitHub Copilot directly to Flare, helping teams set up, execute, and analyze complex computational chemistry workflows in minutes not hours.

Drug discovery teams are under pressure to evaluate more molecules, deliver results faster and achieve more with the resources they already have. AI can help, but scientists do not want another standalone agent to learn, validate and govern. They need a practical way to use the AI tools they already trust within the scientific workflows they rely on every day.

The Flare AI Client is Cresset's answer to that challenge.

Released as part of Flare™ V13, Cresset's platform for molecular design, modeling and analysis, the Flare AI Client enables researchers to use their preferred AI provider such as Claude Code or GitHub Copilot directly within Flare. Scientists can automate workflows and analyze results using the AI tools they already trust, helping turn hours spent operating software into minutes of scientific review.

"The promise of AI in drug discovery is not that it replaces scientists," said Dr Tim Cheeseright, CEO of Cresset. "It's that it removes friction from the work scientists do every day. Whether that's exploring chemical space, generating new molecular ideas or completing routine modeling workflows, our goal is simple: help discovery chemists spend less time operating software and more time making scientific decisions. Chemists don't need another provider. They need their time back."

While AI tools are becoming increasingly common across research organisations, many scientific teams struggle to integrate them into regulated research environments and established molecule discovery workflows. Researchers often move information between multiple applications, manually configure calculations and repeatedly perform routine tasks that add little scientific value.

The Flare AI Client addresses this challenge by enabling AI assistants to interact directly with Flare's molecular design, modeling and analysis capabilities. Using natural language, scientists can set up and execute modeling workflows, explore molecular datasets, generate bespoke analysis scripts and automate routine reporting and data-processing tasks without leaving the platform.

Unlike standalone scientific AI agents, the Flare AI Client allows organisations to connect their existing approved AI assistants directly to Flare's computational chemistry capabilities.

"Scientists already have company-approved AI tools. Rather than asking them to adopt and govern another AI platform, we wanted to make those tools useful within new and existing molecular modeling workflows. The goal isn't more AI. It's helping scientists get more value from the software and data they already use." said Dr Tim Cheeseright, CEO of Cresset.

Activities that previously required multiple manual steps can now be initiated and managed through natural language interactions, making advanced computational chemistry methods more accessible to more scientists. By reducing the effort required to run computational chemistry workflows, the Flare AI Client enables scientists to focus on making better discovery decisions.

The Flare AI Client is available now as part of Flare V13.

data.title: 5 FDA decisions to watch in the fourth quarter of 2026
data.description:
The third quarter of 2026 brought some much-needed stability atop the Food and Drug Administration. 

Acting commissioner Kyle Diamantas steered the organization through a relatively drama-free three months. Advisory committee meetings — the public drug-debate forums that had largely disappeared during former chief Marty Makary’s turbulent tenure — picked up again. And interim leaders at the FDA’s two main “CDER” and “CBER” drug review offices became permanent directors, giving the biopharmaceutical sector the kind of predictability it had craved for much of the previous year. 

Yet still unclear is when the agency’s top position will be filled. White House policy aide Heidi Overton is President Donald Trump’s pick to be the next FDA commissioner and, at a congressional hearing last week, carefully answered thorny questions on vaccines and abortion. But her chances of being confirmed ahead the midterms are uncertain, as there’s an “extremely tight” window before the Senate hits a recess on Oct. 5, wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Brian Abrahams. 

The situation could get complicated if it drags on. A vote during “lame duck sessions” could draw resistance from moderate Republications, and a Democrat-controlled Senate might dim Overton’s chances even more, Abrahams wrote. 

In the meantime, critical decisions lay ahead on a first-of-its-kind cancer immunotherapy, a “functional cure” for hepatitis B and much more. Here are five notable ones that could come during the fourth quarter.

data.title: Biotech IPOs are the industry’s lifeblood. Track how they’re performing.
data.description:
Initial public offerings make the biotechnology industry tick. Stock listings give young companies the funding they need to develop their drugs, and their venture backers an opportunity to earn a return.

For much of the past decade, biotechs found Wall Street receptive to their pitches. Public investment, drawn in by scientific advances and company successes, bolstered generations of new drugmakers.

IPO activity reached a peak in 2021, when more than 100 biotechs priced an initial offering and together raised nearly $15 billion. But that momentum came to a halt in 2022 as stock prices of newly public companies plummeted amid a sector-wide downturn. The pace of IPOs stalled and, last year, only 11 drugmakers priced initial share sales.

Emerging biotechs now face a tougher road to public markets. Which will make it? Which create value and which fail? What types of companies earn the best returns? Who are their investors?

Biopharma Dive is tracking these questions in the database below, which will be updated regularly. If we've missed anything, or there's any additional information you'd like to see, please reach out and let us know.

Editor's note: Click on a company to pull up more information, and scroll to the bottom of the page to read how this information was collected and organized. If tables or values do not display below, please try clearing your browser's cache and reloading the page.

data.title: ACTO Named a Luminary in Everest Group’s “Innovation Watch: Agentic AI in Life Sciences Commercial 2026”
data.description:
TORONTO AND NEW YORK, N.Y. —

Recognition highlights ACTO’s role-based SuperAgents, cross-platform orchestration, and Life Sciences-focused approach to governed agentic AI

ACTO, uniting human intelligence with empathetic AI in Life Sciences, today announced that it has been named a Luminary in Everest Group’s Innovation Watch: Agentic AI in Life Sciences Commercial 2026, a global assessment of leading agentic AI technology providers serving commercial teams in the Life Sciences industry.

The report evaluates 22 providers of agentic AI products and platforms across two dimensions: market performance, which includes scale and maturity, and ecosystem drivers, which includes partnerships and investments. Providers are categorized as Luminaries, Fast Followers, Influencers, or Seekers. ACTO is positioned in the Luminary category, which represents providers with the strongest market performance and ecosystem drivers.

Everest Group’s research comes as agentic AI emerges as a major enabler of commercial transformation across Life Sciences. The report identifies opportunities spanning sales, marketing, medical affairs, market access, and patient services, as organizations look to agentic AI to improve decision-making, automate work, coordinate actions across systems, and enable more personalized engagement. 

“As life sciences enterprises scale agentic AI across commercial functions, the focus is shifting from isolated AI applications to connected commercial platforms that can connect data, content, and workflows across roles and systems. The value of agentic AI will depend on its ability to coordinate activity across systems and functions while preserving governance, traceability, and human accountability,” said Rohit K, Practice Director at Everest Group, “ACTO differentiates through its role-based approach to agentic AI in life sciences commercial, combining domain-specific SuperAgents with cross-platform orchestration and life sciences-focused governance. Its growing partner ecosystem and early customer deployments further support enterprise adoption, positioning ACTO as a Luminary in Everest Group’s Innovation Watch: Agentic AI in Life Sciences Commercial 2026.”

ACTO’s inclusion reflects an AI strategy years in the making. The company began investing in AI in 2022 with LAICA, its AI-powered conversational assistant for Life Sciences learning, which evolved into ACTO SuperAgents, launched in 2026.

“We are thrilled to be named a Luminary by Everest Group, recognized alongside our strategic partners Veeva and Salesforce,” said Parth Khanna, Co-founder and CEO of ACTO. “We began investing in agentic AI in 2022 because we believed AI could fundamentally change how work gets done in Life Sciences, not by replacing people, but by augmenting them. That vision is now a reality. Our customers see tremendous value and impact from role-based SuperAgents that understand the person, the work they do, and the highly regulated environment in which they operate. This recognition reinforces our belief that the future of AI in Life Sciences is not about adding more tools; it’s about creating an intelligent, connected workforce where people and AI work together to achieve better outcomes.”

Built exclusively for Life Sciences, ACTO combines its AI-powered Field Excellence Platform with role-based SuperAgents that work across systems to deliver compliant, in-the-moment support—from clinical and scientific knowledge retrieval to coaching and field medical insight capture—so customer-facing professionals can spend less time navigating systems and more time strengthening relationships with healthcare professionals.

The recognition follows ACTO’s inclusion earlier this year among Everest Group’s Top 50™ Pharmaceutical Technology Providers for 2026, further underscoring the company’s continued investment in AI-powered field excellence and agentic AI purpose-built for Life Sciences.

data.title: SGD Pharma expands its offer in molded and tubular pharmaceutical glass packaging at CPHI Milan 2026
data.description:
PARIS, France —

SGD Pharma, a global market leader in pharmaceutical glass primary packaging solutions and industry trailblazer in sustainability and decarbonization, will present its expanded portfolio of molded and tubular glass products and services on booth 11F17 during CPHI Milan from 6th to 8th October 2026.

  • SGD Pharma will debut MySterinity Nasal, a new range of molded vials extending its established Sterinity approach*. 
    Designed for the growing high-value nasal drug delivery market driven by a rise in biologics with higher microbiological requirements, MySterinity Nasal offers pharmaceutical companies a flexible solution for enhanced quality and safety, as well as improved Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). The Type I U-Save nasal vials can be pre-washed, depyrogenated or sterilized, making them suitable for systemic therapies, CNS therapies, and vaccines. 
  • SGD Pharma also announces the launch of its Ready-to-Use (RTU) tubular vials for sensitive, high-value parenteral drugs. 
    Washed, depyrogenated and sterilized, the new RTU vials support pharmaceutical companies operating in aseptic fill-finish environments and seeking increased quality and safety. The tubular RTU vials will be produced at SGD Pharma’s Felino, Italy ISO 5 environment manufacturing site following its acquisition of Alphial. They will offer speed of delivery, improved TCO and the convenience of a single supplier for their complete range of RTU Type I vials. 
  • SGD Pharma is also launching MySealian, a new GMP-compliant subcontracting service for customers and partners’ vials
    This new service enables any glass manufacturer, pharmaceutical company or OEM to access SGD Pharma’s best-in-class Sealian treatment for their existing ranges of molded glass primary packaging products, with no capital investment. The Sealian internal glass vial treatment preserves the integrity of sensitive therapeutic products by creating a protective barrier coating. Its enhanced hydrophobic properties prevent high viscosity infusions from sticking to the internal surface of the vial, enabling clear product visibility, easy inspection and minimal product waste. 
  • Sealian will now also be available as a treatment option for SDG Pharma’s new tubular vial solutions.

Olivier Rousseau, CEO of SGD Pharma comments: “One year after the acquisition of Alphial, SGD Pharma is well positioned to address the evolving challenges of the pharmaceutical industry, offering innovative products and solutions across both molded and tubular glass primary packaging. We are particularly proud that these innovations are developed within a comprehensive ESG framework, ensuring that sustainability considerations are embedded from the very outset of every project. “

Visit booth 11F17 at CPHI to explore SGD Pharma’s portfolio and meet the team driving the next generation of glass packaging innovations. 

Visit the new website here: http://www.sgd-pharma.com

*SGD Pharma is partnered with SG EZ-fill® to offer washed, depyrogenated and sterilized Type I molded glass vials developed to meet the rigorous requirements of the pharmaceutical industry, speed up time to market and reduce total cost of ownership because of increased quality and flexibility.

data.title: Woven Health Collective Wins Inaugural 2026 MM+M Award for Generative AI and Synthetic Media
data.description:
NEW YORK —

Woven Health Collective announced that it won the 2026 MM+M award: Use of Generative AI (GenAI) and Synthetic Media award. The award recognizes Woven’s Imagination Through Science campaign, which used generative AI to transform scientifically inspired structures into immersive, couture-like environments around real human subjects. 

“AI expanded what was creatively possible, but technology was never the idea,” said Dennis Leahy, Chief Creative Officer at Woven Health Collective. “The idea was to make science something you could experience, to give it texture, emotion, and dimension. To transform the complexity of science into something people could not only understand, but feel.”

The team used a studio photoshoot and technical details such as lighting, lens, depth of field, and color temperature to create a visual language that extended across print, digital, video, and social channels.
